cards.title: Temporal vs Queues
cards.question: Why move 9 integrations onto a workflow engine like Temporal instead of chaining jobs on a queue?
points: Durable execution: state is saved as an event history, so a workflow resumes exactly where it stopped after a crash
Retries, timeouts and backoff are declared per activity, not hand-written for each integration
Long waits (hours or days) are built in, so no polling jobs or cron glue
Every run has an inspectable history, which makes debugging and on-call much easier
Cost: a new mental model, and workflow code must be deterministic
cards.weakness: Why must Temporal workflow code be deterministic?

cards.title: The Temporal Migration
cards.question: Tell me about leading Fynd's first Temporal rollout: 9 integrations and about 80 workflow stages in 9 to 12 months.
points: Situation: each marketplace integration had grown its own special cases over years
Task: you led the company's first Temporal adoption and owned the shared workflow model
Action: be ready to explain the shared model and how you moved integrations over one at a time
Result: 9 integrations and ~80 stages on one model, replacing per-integration special cases
Close with one lesson and what you would do differently
cards.weakness: How did you migrate live sellers without breaking their order flow?

cards.title: Determinism
cards.question: Why must Temporal workflow code be deterministic?
points: After a crash, a worker rebuilds workflow state by replaying the event history
Replay must issue the same commands in the same order, or Temporal flags a non-determinism error
So no Date.now(), Math.random() or direct I/O inside workflows
Side effects go in activities; use the workflow APIs for time and sleep
Changing running workflows needs versioning (patching)
cards.weakness: How do you change workflow code while old runs are still in flight?

cards.title: Workflows & Activities
cards.question: In Temporal, what is the difference between a workflow and an activity?
points: Workflow: the orchestration logic. Deterministic and durable
Activity: the real work with side effects (API calls, DB writes). Allowed to fail
Activities are retried by a retry policy with backoff
Timeouts: start-to-close, schedule-to-close, heartbeat
Workers poll task queues to run both
cards.weakness: What is an activity heartbeat for?

cards.title: Per-Seller Rate Limits
cards.question: How do you respect Amazon, Flipkart and Shopify rate limits while syncing catalogues of up to 300,000 SKUs?
points: Limits apply per seller credential, so throttle per seller, not globally
Queue the work and let workers pull only at the allowed rate (token bucket)
On 429, honour Retry-After and back off exponentially with jitter
Batch updates into feeds instead of one call per SKU
Only sync what changed since the last run
cards.weakness: What is jitter, and why add it to backoff?

cards.title: Silent Schema Change
cards.question: A marketplace quietly changes its API response format. How do you find out before your sellers do?
points: Validate responses at the boundary against a schema and fail loudly
Contract tests against the OpenAPI spec (Specmatic) catch drift in CI
Alert on spikes in parse or validation errors per marketplace
Tolerate unknown extra fields, fail on missing required ones
Pin API versions where the marketplace supports it
cards.weakness: Strict or tolerant parsing: which do you pick and why?

cards.title: Multi-Market Sync
cards.question: Design inventory and order sync for a seller with 300,000 SKUs across Amazon, Flipkart and Shopify.
points: Postgres is the source of truth; track changes so you only push deltas
One adapter per marketplace behind a shared interface
A queue per seller and marketplace that respects rate limits and batches feeds
Idempotent upserts on external IDs, retries with backoff, dead-letter queue
A reconciliation job compares counts to catch drift; metrics per seller
cards.weakness: Two marketplaces sell the last unit at the same moment. What happens?

cards.title: Amazon VDF in 3 Months
cards.question: You delivered the company's first Amazon VDF integration in 3 months. Walk me through it.
points: VDF = Vendor Direct Fulfillment: the vendor ships Amazon orders straight to customers
Started from a design document: scope, order and shipment flows, risks
Explain how the shared workflow model sped things up
Milestones that kept it on track from design to production
Result: first VDF integration live in 3 months
cards.weakness: What was the riskiest part, and how did you de-risk it?

cards.title: 70k Orders a Day
cards.question: Explain your BullMQ and Kafka pipeline: 70,000+ orders and feed updates a day within Amazon's feed limits, without delaying new orders.
points: Kafka carries the durable, replayable stream of order and inventory events
Consumers turn events into BullMQ jobs, which handle retries and rate limiting
Priorities: new orders jump ahead of bulk feed updates
Many updates are batched into one feed submission to stay under limits
70k a day averages ~0.8 per second, but peaks are bursty, so you buffer
cards.weakness: Why both Kafka and BullMQ? Couldn't one do both jobs?

cards.title: Kafka vs BullMQ
cards.question: Kafka and BullMQ both move messages. What is each one good at?
points: Kafka: a partitioned log. Many consumer groups, replay, ordering per partition, huge throughput
Kafka has no per-message retry, delay or priority built in
BullMQ: a job queue on Redis with per-job retries, delays, priorities and a rate limiter
Use Kafka to fan events out between services
Use BullMQ to execute tasks with throttling and retries
cards.weakness: How does Kafka guarantee ordering?

cards.title: 0% to 70% Coverage
cards.question: You introduced the team's first automated tests for 9 integrations that had 0% coverage. How?
points: Situation: no tests, so third-party changes caused regressions
Jest and Mocha unit tests for mapping and business logic
Specmatic contract tests generated from the OpenAPI specs
A 70% coverage gate in Azure DevOps CI so it stayed enforced
How you got buy-in and chose what to test first (riskiest code)
cards.weakness: Is 70% a good coverage target? What does coverage not tell you?

cards.title: SSO & Seller Auth
cards.question: You set up Google SSO and per-seller IAM authentication for Amazon's APIs across 100+ sellers. Explain both.
points: Google SSO: OpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2.0; Google returns an ID token
Each seller authorises the app, which stores credentials per seller
Short-lived access tokens are refreshed from stored refresh tokens
Credentials are encrypted and strictly scoped to one seller
Least-privilege IAM roles for API access
cards.weakness: Where did you store per-seller secrets, and how were they rotated?

cards.title: On-Call Incident
cards.question: Tell me about a production incident you handled on-call.
points: Pick your best one of the 30+ and practise it until it is crisp
How it was detected and who was affected
Mitigate first: how you stopped the bleeding
Root cause, and how you talked to the client throughout
The RCA you wrote and what changed afterwards
cards.weakness: What makes a root cause analysis actually useful?

cards.title: Root Cause Analysis
cards.question: What goes into a good root cause analysis (postmortem)?
points: Timeline of what happened and when
Impact: who was affected and for how long
Root cause, found by asking why repeatedly (5 whys)
Action items with owners and dates
Blameless: focus on systems, not people
cards.weakness: Why should postmortems be blameless?

cards.title: No-Code Builder
cards.question: You built a no-code workflow builder used daily by 5+ product managers. Tell me about it.
points: Problem: every new integration needed engineering time
Built with React, TypeScript and React Flow
Iterated with the PMs who used it every day
Result: new integrations needed 50% less engineering help
Be ready to say how the 50% was measured
cards.weakness: What feedback from the PMs changed the design the most?

cards.title: Workflow Platform
cards.question: Walk me through your Workflow Automation Platform.
points: No-code: users chain API calls on a drag-and-drop React Flow canvas
4 node types: triggers, conditions, loops and actions
The graph is saved as JSON and executed on Temporal
Retries and step-by-step tracing for every run
100/100 runs of a 20-step workflow passed against an API failing 30% of calls
cards.weakness: How do you turn a graph on a canvas into something executable?

cards.title: Running the Graph
cards.question: How do you safely execute a user-drawn graph with conditions and loops?
points: Validate first: one trigger, no dangling edges, cycles only through loop nodes
Walk from the trigger, following edges
Condition nodes choose which outgoing edge to follow
Loop nodes get a max-iteration guard so nothing runs forever
Each action is a Temporal activity with its own retry policy; record inputs and outputs per step
cards.weakness: How would you add parallel branches?

cards.title: 100 out of 100
cards.question: How did you prove the platform survives failures?
points: A mock API failed 30% of calls at random
Ran a 20-step workflow 100 times; all 100 completed
Without retries, all 20 steps succeeding is 0.7^20, about 0.08%
Retries with backoff on every step made the difference
Killed the server mid-run; Temporal resumed from the event history
cards.weakness: What would break if the mock API calls were not idempotent?

cards.title: React Flow
cards.question: What is React Flow, and how do custom nodes work?
points: A library for node-based UIs: nodes, edges and handles
State is arrays of nodes and edges, updated via onNodesChange and onEdgesChange
Custom nodes are React components registered in a nodeTypes map
Handles are the connection points on a node
isValidConnection can block invalid links
cards.weakness: How do you keep a large canvas fast?

cards.title: Four Node Types
cards.question: Why triggers, conditions, loops and actions? Why those four?
points: Trigger: starts a run (webhook, schedule or manual)
Action: does the work, usually an API call
Condition: branches the flow
Loop: repeats over a list
Together they cover sequence, branching and iteration
cards.weakness: What node type would you add next, and why?

cards.title: Zero Lost Events
cards.question: Walk me through how FormHook makes sure no webhook event is lost when an endpoint fails.
points: Each event is saved as a BullMQ job in Redis before any delivery is attempted
Up to 3 attempts with exponential backoff, giving a flaky endpoint time to recover
After the last failure the job moves to a dead-letter queue to inspect and replay
A failure-simulation mode injects errors and timeouts to prove recovery works
Runs on EC2, provisioned with Terraform for one-command setup and teardown
cards.weakness: The endpoint got your request but timed out replying. What stops a duplicate delivery?

cards.title: Duplicate Delivery
cards.question: The endpoint received your webhook but timed out before replying, so you retry. How do you stop it being processed twice?
points: Exactly-once delivery over a network is not possible; aim for at-least-once
Send a unique event ID (idempotency key) with every delivery
The receiver stores seen IDs and ignores repeats
Retries reuse the same ID
Document this so receivers know to dedupe
cards.weakness: How long should a receiver remember event IDs?

cards.title: Exponential Backoff
cards.question: Why use exponential backoff instead of retrying straight away?
points: Gives a failing service time to recover
Avoids a retry storm hammering a struggling endpoint
Delays grow: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s
Add jitter so clients do not all retry at the same instant
Cap the max delay and the number of attempts
cards.weakness: What is the thundering herd problem?

cards.title: Dead-Letter Queue
cards.question: What is a dead-letter queue, and why have one?
points: Holds messages that failed every retry
Stops a poison message from blocking the queue
Keeps the data so nothing is silently lost
Inspect, fix, then replay
Alert when it starts filling up
cards.weakness: What is a poison message?

cards.title: Failure Simulation
cards.question: Why build a failure-simulation mode into FormHook itself?
points: Chaos engineering on a small scale: break things on purpose
Proves retries and the dead-letter queue actually work
Makes timeouts and errors reproducible in tests
Cheaper than waiting for a real outage to find bugs
Must be impossible to switch on by accident in production
cards.weakness: How do you make sure failure simulation can never run in production?

cards.title: Signed Webhooks
cards.question: How does a webhook receiver know a request really came from you?
points: Sign the body with HMAC using a shared secret and send it in a header
The receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares
Use a constant-time comparison
Include a timestamp and reject old requests to stop replays
Always over HTTPS
cards.weakness: Why does the comparison need to be constant-time?

cards.title: Leitner System
cards.question: How does this app decide when you see a card again?
points: Five boxes, shown as foils from Plain to Full Art
Got it: up one box. Not yet: back to box 1
Higher boxes wait longer before the next review
Harder rarities get shorter waits, so you see them more
Spacing reviews out beats cramming (the spacing effect)
cards.weakness: Why does reviewing just before you forget work so well?

cards.title: Row Level Security
cards.question: What is Row Level Security in Postgres, and how does Supabase use it?
points: Policies on a table decide which rows each user can see or change
USING filters reads; WITH CHECK validates writes
auth.uid() comes from the user's JWT
That is why the publishable key can be public
Wrap auth.uid() in a SELECT so it is evaluated once per query
cards.weakness: Why does an UPDATE policy also need WITH CHECK?

cards.title: Supabase vs Firebase
cards.question: Why did you build this app on Supabase instead of Firebase?
points: Supabase is Postgres: SQL, joins, constraints, RLS
Firebase Firestore is a NoSQL document store
Supabase is open source and self-hostable: low lock-in
Firebase has built-in offline sync and never pauses
SQL skills carry over to almost any backend job
cards.weakness: How would you add offline support to this app?

cards.title: The Streak Query
cards.question: Write the SQL that computes a daily streak from a table of pack openings.
points: Get the distinct local dates with at least one opening
Gaps and islands: date minus row_number() is constant for consecutive days
Group by that value to get each run of days
Take the run that ends today or yesterday
Its length is the current streak
cards.weakness: How do time zones break a naive streak query?

cards.title: Definer vs Invoker
cards.question: SECURITY DEFINER vs SECURITY INVOKER functions in Postgres?
points: Definer runs with the function owner's rights and bypasses RLS
Invoker runs as the caller, so RLS still applies
Definer functions in an exposed schema can be called by anyone
Prefer invoker; if you need definer, check auth.uid() inside
Always set search_path on functions
cards.weakness: Why set search_path on a function?

cards.title: PWA
cards.question: What makes a web app a Progressive Web App?
points: A web manifest: name, icons, standalone display
A service worker for caching and offline
Served over HTTPS
Installable to the home screen like a native app
cards.weakness: What can a service worker do that a normal page cannot?

cards.title: The Card Flip
cards.question: How does the 3D card flip in this app work?
points: perspective on the parent gives depth
transform-style: preserve-3d keeps children in 3D space
backface-visibility: hidden hides each face when turned away
The back face starts rotated 180 degrees
Rotating the container shows one face, then the other
cards.weakness: Why animate transform instead of width or top?

cards.title: The Pack Builder
cards.question: How does the pack builder pick cards, and why do hard cards show up more?
points: Five slots: Common, Flex, Rare, Rare, Ultra Rare
Each slot takes the right rarity: due cards first, then new ones
Flex takes the most overdue card of any rarity
Falls back to other rarities when a slot runs dry
Harder rarities have shorter review waits, so they come back sooner
cards.weakness: How would you test the pack builder?

cards.title: TS Types
cards.question: TypeScript: interface vs type, and what is a generic?
points: Both describe object shapes
Interfaces can be extended and merged
Type aliases also handle unions, intersections and mapped types
Generics are type parameters: function first<T>(items: T[]): T
Prefer unknown over any: it forces you to check before use
cards.weakness: unknown vs any?

cards.title: Narrowing
cards.question: What are discriminated unions and type narrowing?
points: A union where every member has a shared literal field, like kind
Checking that field (switch or if) narrows to one member
Exhaustiveness: assign the leftover to never to catch missed cases
Other guards: typeof, in, instanceof
Custom guards: function isOrder(x): x is Order
cards.weakness: How do you make the compiler catch a switch that misses a case?

cards.title: Closures
cards.question: What is a closure? Give a real use.
points: A function remembers variables from the scope where it was created
Private state and factory functions
Event handlers and callbacks
Memoization caches
In React, closures cause stale state bugs
cards.weakness: What is a stale closure in React, and how do you fix it?

cards.title: Promise Combinators
cards.question: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any?
points: all: resolves when all succeed, rejects on the first failure
allSettled: waits for every promise and reports each status
race: settles with whichever settles first
any: resolves with the first success
For 300,000 items, limit concurrency (batches or p-limit)
cards.weakness: How do you run 10,000 API calls but only 10 at a time?

cards.title: Re-renders
cards.question: What triggers a React re-render, and how do you avoid unnecessary ones?
points: Triggers: state change, parent re-render, context value change
Reconciliation diffs the new tree against the old; keys identify list items
memo, useMemo and useCallback skip work when inputs are unchanged
Keep state close to where it is used; split big contexts
React Compiler can memoize automatically
cards.weakness: Why is an array index a bad key?

cards.title: useEffect
cards.question: What is useEffect for, and what are common mistakes?
points: Syncing with things outside React: subscriptions, timers, fetching, the DOM
The dependency array controls when it re-runs
Return a cleanup function to undo the effect
Mistake: computing derived state in an effect instead of during render
Mistake: missing dependencies, or loops that set state every run
cards.weakness: Why does my effect run twice in development?

cards.title: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR
cards.question: In Next.js, what are CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR, and when do you use each?
points: CSR: the browser renders; slower first paint and weaker SEO
SSR: the server renders each request; always fresh
SSG: HTML built once at build time; fastest
ISR: static pages re-generated in the background on a timer
App Router adds React Server Components
cards.weakness: What is hydration?

cards.title: Do I Need Redux?
cards.question: When do you need Redux instead of React state or context?
points: Local state for local concerns
Context for rarely-changing globals: theme, current user
Redux Toolkit for complex shared state, devtools and middleware
Server data is often better in a fetching library like TanStack Query
Redux: one store, actions, pure reducers
cards.weakness: Why must reducers be pure?

cards.title: Vue vs React
cards.question: Vue 3 vs React: what are the key differences?
points: Vue tracks reactive dependencies with proxies and updates only what changed
React re-runs components and diffs the output
Vue uses templates by default; React uses JSX
Vue's setup() runs once; React hooks run on every render
Both are component-based with similar ecosystems
cards.weakness: How does Vue's reactivity know what to update?

cards.title: Tailwind CSS
cards.question: What is Tailwind, and what is the main criticism of it?
points: Utility-first: small single-purpose classes like p-4 and flex
A design scale keeps spacing and colours consistent
Only the classes you use end up in the CSS
Criticism: long class lists in markup
Fix: extract repeated patterns into components
cards.weakness: How do you avoid repeating the same long class list everywhere?

cards.title: The Event Loop
cards.question: Explain the Node.js event loop.
points: JavaScript runs on one thread; I/O is non-blocking via libuv
Phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll (I/O), check (setImmediate), close
Microtasks (process.nextTick, then promises) run between callbacks
libuv's thread pool handles fs, crypto and DNS work
CPU-heavy code blocks everything: move it to worker threads or a job queue
cards.weakness: In what order do setTimeout(0), setImmediate, Promise.then and process.nextTick run?

cards.title: One Slow Request
cards.question: One CPU-heavy request makes your whole Node API slow. Why, and how do you fix it?
points: It blocks the single event-loop thread, so every request waits
Move the work to worker_threads
Or push it to a background job queue
Or split it into chunks that yield back to the loop
Monitor event-loop lag to catch it
cards.weakness: Cluster mode vs worker threads: what is the difference?

cards.title: Express Middleware
cards.question: How does Express middleware work?
points: Functions (req, res, next) that run in the order they are registered
next() passes control on; next(err) jumps to error handlers
Error handlers take 4 arguments (err, req, res, next)
Used for parsing, auth, logging, CORS
Express 5 forwards rejected promises; Express 4 needs you to call next(err)
cards.weakness: Give an example where middleware order breaks something.

cards.title: Vite vs Webpack
cards.question: Why is Vite so much faster than Webpack in development?
points: Webpack bundles the whole app before it can serve it
Vite serves native ES modules, and the browser asks for files as needed
Dependencies are pre-bundled once
Hot updates replace only the changed module
Production builds are still bundled for speed
cards.weakness: Why does Vite still bundle for production?

cards.title: Jest vs Mocha
cards.question: Jest vs Mocha?
points: Jest: all-in-one runner, assertions, mocks, coverage and snapshots
Mocha: just the runner; add Chai, Sinon and nyc
Jest runs test files in parallel workers
Vitest is the natural pick for Vite projects
cards.weakness: How do you mock a third-party API in Jest?

cards.title: Bias vs Variance
cards.question: Explain bias vs variance, and overfitting.
points: High bias: too simple, underfits (bad on train and test)
High variance: too complex, overfits (great on train, bad on test)
A big gap between train and validation error signals overfitting
Fixes: more data, regularization (L2, dropout), simpler model, early stopping
Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate
cards.weakness: How do you detect overfitting during training?

cards.title: Train, Val, Test
cards.question: Why separate train, validation and test sets?
points: Train: fit the model
Validation: tune hyperparameters and choose models
Test: one final, unbiased estimate; touch it once
Data leakage makes results look better than reality
k-fold cross-validation when data is scarce
cards.weakness: Give an example of data leakage.

cards.title: Precision & Recall
cards.question: Precision, recall and F1: when does accuracy lie?
points: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of what you flagged, how much was right
Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of what was there, how much you found
F1 is their harmonic mean
With 99% negatives, predicting all negative scores 99% accuracy
Choose by the cost of false positives vs false negatives
cards.weakness: Spam filter: optimise precision or recall?

cards.title: Big-O Basics
cards.question: Big-O of common operations: hash map, sorted array, heap, sorting?
points: Hash map: O(1) average lookup and insert, O(n) worst case
Sorted array: O(log n) binary search, O(n) insert
Heap: O(log n) push and pop, O(1) peek
Comparison sorting: O(n log n)
cards.weakness: When does a hash map degrade to O(n)?

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.question: Explain backpropagation and gradient descent.
points: Forward pass computes predictions and the loss
Backprop applies the chain rule to get gradients layer by layer, backwards
Gradient descent moves weights against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate
Mini-batch SGD and Adam in practice
Vanishing gradients: helped by ReLU, residual connections, normalization
cards.weakness: What happens if the learning rate is too high or too low?

cards.title: Attention
cards.question: How does attention work in a Transformer?
points: Tokens become embeddings plus position information
Each token is projected into a query, key and value
Attention = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V: each token weighs every other token
Multi-head: several attention patterns in parallel
Stacked with feed-forward layers, residuals and layer norm; parallel, unlike RNNs
cards.weakness: Why divide by the square root of d?

cards.title: PyTorch vs TF
cards.question: PyTorch vs TensorFlow?
points: PyTorch: eager and Pythonic; the research default
TensorFlow and Keras: strong production tooling (Serving, Lite)
Both compile graphs when needed (torch.compile, tf.function)
Both export to ONNX
cards.weakness: What does model.eval() change in PyTorch?

cards.title: Keyword vs Dense
cards.question: Information retrieval: BM25 keyword search vs dense embeddings?
points: TF-IDF: term frequency times inverse document frequency
BM25 adds term saturation and document length normalization
Dense embeddings capture meaning; search by nearest neighbour
Hybrid search combines both and is common in practice
Evaluate with precision@k, MAP, nDCG
cards.weakness: When does keyword search beat embeddings?

cards.title: Model Serving
cards.question: ONNX Runtime, TensorRT and Triton: what does each one do?
points: ONNX: a portable model format; ONNX Runtime runs it on many kinds of hardware
TensorRT: NVIDIA's GPU optimizer (layer fusion, FP16 and INT8)
Triton Inference Server: serves models over HTTP or gRPC
Triton adds dynamic batching and hosts many models at once
Typical path: train in PyTorch, export to ONNX, optimize, serve
cards.weakness: What does quantization trade away?

cards.title: Indexes
cards.question: How does a database index work, and what does it cost?
points: Usually a B-tree: a sorted structure, so lookups are O(log n) instead of a full scan
Composite index column order matters (leftmost prefix rule)
Costs: slower writes and extra storage
Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Partial and covering indexes for special cases
cards.weakness: With an index on (a, b), does WHERE b = ? use it?

cards.title: ACID & Isolation
cards.question: What does ACID mean, and what are isolation levels?
points: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable
Read committed is Postgres's default
Repeatable read and serializable are stricter
Anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks rows you are about to change
cards.weakness: What is a phantom read?

cards.title: The Last Unit
cards.question: One unit left, two orders at the same instant. Design it so you never oversell.
points: Atomic conditional update: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0
Check rows affected: 0 means sold out
Or lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction
Or optimistic locking with a version column
Across marketplaces: keep a safety buffer and sync stock quickly
cards.weakness: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: when do you use each?

cards.title: 300k Upserts
cards.question: Syncing 300,000 SKUs into Postgres: how do you write that efficiently?
points: Batch writes (multi-row INSERT or COPY), never row by row
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE for upserts
Skip unchanged rows (compare a hash or updated_at)
Commit in chunks of a few thousand rows
A unique index on the conflict key
cards.weakness: Why not do all 300,000 rows in one giant transaction?

cards.title: Pagination
cards.question: Offset vs cursor pagination?
points: OFFSET scans and throws away rows, so deep pages get slow
Offsets also skip or repeat rows when data changes
Cursor (keyset): WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n
Fast and stable with an index
Trade-off: no jumping straight to page 50
cards.weakness: How do you build a cursor when sorting by a non-unique column like created_at?

cards.title: Postgres vs MongoDB
cards.question: Postgres vs MongoDB: how do you choose?
points: Postgres: schemas, joins, constraints, ACID transactions
MongoDB: flexible documents, nested data, built-in sharding
Postgres JSONB gives you some document flexibility too
Decide by access patterns and how much consistency you need
Orders and inventory are relational and need transactions
cards.weakness: When would MongoDB clearly be the better choice?

cards.title: N+1 Queries
cards.question: What is the N+1 query problem in Sequelize or Mongoose?
points: 1 query for a list, then 1 more query per item
Caused by ORMs lazy-loading relations
Fix: eager loading (include in Sequelize, populate in Mongoose)
Or a single join, or batching (DataLoader)
Spot it in query logs or APM traces
cards.weakness: How would you spot N+1 queries in production?

cards.title: ORM vs Raw SQL
cards.question: ORM (Sequelize, Mongoose) vs raw SQL?
points: ORM: productivity, models, validation, migrations
ORM hides the queries, which can surprise you on performance
Raw SQL: full control for complex or hot queries
A mix is common: ORM by default, raw SQL for hot paths
Query builders sit in the middle
cards.weakness: What is a migration, and why version it?

cards.title: REST Design
cards.question: What makes an API RESTful?
points: Resources are nouns in URLs: /orders/42
HTTP methods carry meaning: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
Stateless: each request carries everything needed
Plus pagination, versioning and an OpenAPI spec
cards.weakness: PUT vs PATCH?

cards.title: Idempotency
cards.question: What is idempotency, and why does it matter for retries?
points: Doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not
Idempotency keys: the client sends a key, the server stores and replays the result
Essential with retries and at-least-once delivery
Upserts on external IDs make syncs idempotent
cards.weakness: Where do you store idempotency keys, and for how long?

cards.title: OAuth 2.0
cards.question: Walk through the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.
points: App redirects the user to the auth server with client_id, scopes, redirect_uri and state
User logs in and consents; the auth server redirects back with a code
The backend exchanges the code (plus secret or PKCE verifier) for tokens
Short-lived access token; refresh token to get new ones
OpenID Connect adds an ID token for identity, which is how Google SSO works
cards.weakness: What is PKCE, and what attack does it stop?

cards.title: AuthN vs AuthZ
cards.question: Authentication vs authorization?
points: Authentication: who are you? (login, SSO, tokens)
Authorization: what are you allowed to do? (roles, permissions, row-level rules)
OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization; OIDC adds authentication
401 Unauthorized really means not authenticated
403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed
cards.weakness: Is a JWT for authentication or authorization?

cards.title: Real-Time Options
cards.question: WebSockets vs polling vs Server-Sent Events: when do you use each?
points: Polling: simple, but wasteful and laggy
SSE: one-way server-to-client over plain HTTP, with auto-reconnect
WebSockets: full-duplex over one persistent connection
WebSockets suit chat, live collaboration and games
Scaling WebSockets needs sticky sessions or a pub/sub layer like Redis
cards.weakness: How do you scale WebSockets across several servers?

cards.title: OpenAPI
cards.question: What is OpenAPI, and how did you use it?
points: A machine-readable spec of a REST API: paths, schemas, auth
Generates docs, client SDKs and server stubs
Specmatic uses it as the source of truth for contract tests
Design-first (spec first) vs code-first (generate from code)
cards.weakness: Design-first or code-first: which do you prefer, and why?

cards.title: Rate Limiting
cards.question: Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket rate limiting?
points: Fixed window: simple, but allows bursts at window edges
Sliding window: smoother and fairer
Token bucket: refills at a steady rate and allows bursts up to the bucket size
Across many servers, keep the counters in Redis
Reply 429 with a Retry-After header
cards.weakness: How would you rate limit across 5 API servers?

cards.title: Redis
cards.question: What is Redis, and why does BullMQ need it?
points: In-memory key-value store: very fast reads and writes, with optional persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF log)
Rich data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams
BullMQ keeps every job and its state in Redis: lists for waiting jobs, sorted sets for delayed ones
Atomic Lua scripts mean two workers can never grab the same job
cards.weakness: What happens to your queued jobs if Redis restarts?

cards.title: Redis Restarts
cards.question: Redis restarts. What happens to the jobs in your BullMQ queues?
points: Without persistence, everything in memory is gone
AOF with fsync every second loses at most about a second of writes
RDB snapshots lose everything since the last snapshot
BullMQ needs maxmemory-policy noeviction so Redis never drops job keys
Use replicas or a managed Redis for high availability
cards.weakness: Why must maxmemory-policy be noeviction for BullMQ?

cards.title: Kafka Basics
cards.question: Explain Kafka topics, partitions and consumer groups.
points: A topic is a named log split into partitions
Order is only guaranteed within a partition; the message key picks the partition
In a consumer group, each partition is read by one consumer, which is how you scale
Offsets track each group's position and are committed
Messages are kept for a retention period, so you can replay
cards.weakness: What happens if you add more consumers than partitions?

cards.title: Delivery Guarantees
cards.question: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: how does each happen in Kafka?
points: Commit the offset before processing: at-most-once (a crash loses the message)
Commit after processing: at-least-once (a crash causes duplicates)
Exactly-once inside Kafka: idempotent producer plus transactions
End to end, side effects outside Kafka still need idempotent consumers
Most real systems choose at-least-once plus idempotency
cards.weakness: Which did your pipeline use, and how did you handle duplicates?

cards.title: BullMQ
cards.question: How does BullMQ work?
points: A Queue adds jobs; Workers process them
Job states: waiting, active, delayed, completed, failed
Job options: attempts, backoff, priority, delay
Per-worker concurrency and a built-in rate limiter (max jobs per duration)
Workers hold a lock on active jobs; if it lapses, the job is marked stalled and retried
cards.weakness: What is a stalled job, and what causes one?

cards.title: Event-Driven
cards.question: Event-driven architecture vs direct API calls: pros and cons?
points: Producers and consumers are decoupled and scale on their own
Queues absorb traffic spikes
A consumer being down does not block the producer
Costs: eventual consistency and harder debugging
You must handle ordering, duplicates and event schema changes
cards.weakness: How do you debug a request that hops through 4 services and 2 queues?

cards.title: The Dual Write
cards.question: You save an order to Postgres, then publish an event to Kafka. The publish fails after the commit. Now what?
points: The dual-write problem: two systems, no shared transaction
Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction
A relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka (polling, or CDC such as Debezium)
Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent
Mark or delete outbox rows once published
cards.weakness: Why not publish to Kafka first and then write to the database?

cards.title: Temporal
cards.question: Explain Temporal in one minute.
points: A durable execution platform: you write workflows as ordinary code
The Temporal server stores every workflow's event history
Your workers run the workflow and activity code
Retries and timeouts are configuration, not hand-written loops
Signals push data into a running workflow; queries read its state
cards.weakness: Signal vs query: what is the difference?

cards.title: Monolith or Micro?
cards.question: When would you NOT use microservices?
points: Small team or early product: a monolith ships faster
Every service adds deploys, networking and monitoring overhead
Distributed failures and cross-service consistency are hard
A modular monolith is a good middle ground
Split when parts need independent scaling, deploys or teams
cards.weakness: How do services share data without sharing a database?

cards.title: Docker
cards.question: Container vs VM, and what is inside a Docker image?
points: Containers share the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and cgroups
Much lighter than VMs, which each run a full OS
An image is a stack of read-only layers built from a Dockerfile
Layers are cached, so instruction order matters
Multi-stage builds keep images small
cards.weakness: Why copy package.json and run npm install before copying the source?

cards.title: Kubernetes
cards.question: What are Pods, Deployments, Services and Ingress in Kubernetes?
points: Pod: the smallest unit, one or more containers
Deployment: keeps N replicas running and does rolling updates
Service: a stable address that load-balances across pods
Ingress: routes HTTP traffic into services
ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration
cards.weakness: Liveness probe vs readiness probe?

cards.title: Helm
cards.question: What does Helm add on top of Kubernetes?
points: A package manager for Kubernetes
Charts are templated manifests
values.yaml files per environment
Releases can be upgraded and rolled back
cards.weakness: How do you keep secrets out of values files?

cards.title: Terraform
cards.question: How does Terraform work, and what is state?
points: Declarative infrastructure as code
plan shows the diff; apply makes the changes
The state file maps your config to real resources
Teams use remote state with locking
destroy tears it all down, as in FormHook
cards.weakness: What happens if two people run terraform apply at the same time?

cards.title: CI/CD
cards.question: What should a CI/CD pipeline do?
points: On every push or PR: install, lint, test, coverage gate, build
Produce artifacts or container images
Deploy to environments, with approvals for production
Fail fast and cache dependencies
You used Azure DevOps, GitLab CI and Jenkins
cards.weakness: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment?

cards.title: S3 & EC2
cards.question: What are AWS S3 and EC2, and when do you use each?
points: EC2: virtual servers you manage (OS, patching, scaling)
S3: object storage, very durable and cheap
S3 for files, static assets and backups
Security groups control network access to EC2
IAM roles let EC2 reach S3 without hardcoded keys
cards.weakness: How does an EC2 instance get S3 access without keys in the code?

cards.title: 10x Overnight
cards.question: Your API traffic grows 10x overnight. What breaks first, and what do you do?
points: Find the bottleneck with metrics: CPU, DB connections, queue depth
Stateless app servers scale out behind a load balancer
Database: connection pooling, indexes, read replicas, caching in Redis
Queues absorb spikes; rate limits and backpressure protect the core
Third-party API limits do not scale with you
cards.weakness: Why is the database usually the hardest part to scale?

cards.title: Contract Testing
cards.question: What is contract testing (Specmatic), and how is it different from integration testing?
points: Checks that both sides agree on the API contract (the OpenAPI spec)
Specmatic generates tests from the spec and can stub the provider
Catches breaking changes without running the whole system
Faster and more focused than end-to-end tests
Consumer-driven vs provider-driven contracts
cards.weakness: If the contract itself is wrong, what will contract tests catch?

cards.title: Test Pyramid
cards.question: What is the testing pyramid?
points: Many fast unit tests at the base
Fewer integration tests in the middle
A few slow end-to-end tests at the top
Balances speed, cost and confidence
For integrations: unit tests for mapping logic, contract tests for APIs
cards.weakness: When do mocks give you false confidence?

cards.title: 100% Coverage
cards.question: Does 100% test coverage mean the code is bug-free?
points: No: coverage shows code ran, not that behaviour was checked
Edge cases and bad inputs can still be missing
Branch coverage is stricter than line coverage
Mutation testing measures how good the tests are
Focus coverage on risky code
cards.weakness: What is mutation testing?

cards.title: OpenTelemetry
cards.question: What is OpenTelemetry: traces, metrics and logs?
points: A vendor-neutral standard and SDKs for telemetry
Traces: spans across services, linked by a propagated trace ID
Metrics: counters, gauges, histograms
Logs correlated with traces by trace ID
Exporters send data to backends such as Grafana
cards.weakness: How does a trace ID follow a message through Kafka?

cards.title: Dashboards & Alerts
cards.question: What would you put on a Grafana dashboard, and alert on, for an integration service?
points: Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
Queue depth and the age of the oldest job
429 and 5xx rates per marketplace
Sync lag per seller
Alert on user-facing symptoms; avoid noisy alerts
cards.weakness: What makes an alert actionable?
